Tirshatha
tir-shä'thä
n. (a Persian title of office, rendered in the Authorized Version as the style of the governor of Judah under the great king — borne by Zerubbabel and by Nehemiah)
A Persian loan-word taken into Hebrew as Tirshatha, generally derived from an Old Persian root meaning to be feared or revered — hence his excellency. It is not a name but a style, always written with the article: the Tirshatha.

Biblical Definition

Tirshatha is one of the handful of foreign administrative words the Authorized Version carries over untranslated, and it marks a precise historical situation: Judah after the captivity was not a kingdom but a province, and the man over it held his commission from a Gentile emperor. The title first appears in the register of the returned: “And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim” (Ezr 2:63). That is a governor ruling on a question of ceremonial purity — certain families could not prove their priestly descent, and the Tirshatha suspended their privileges rather than presume. Nehemiah is named with the title outright: “And Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha, and Ezra the priest the scribe, and the Levites that taught the people, said unto all the people, This day is holy unto the LORD your God” (Neh 8:9), and he signs the covenant at its head, “Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah” (Neh 10:1). The office is real civil authority: he levied nothing for himself, he rebuilt a wall, he enforced the sabbath at the gates. But it is authority held under Artaxerxes, and the word itself is a Persian word. Every time the Chronicler writes Tirshatha instead of king, he is confessing that the throne of David stood empty and that the people were still, in the words of Nehemiah's own prayer, servants in the land God gave their fathers.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Tirshatha; it is the Persian title of the governor of Judah after the captivity, borne by Zerubbabel and by Nehemiah.

expand to see more

TIRSHATHA, n. A title of office, of Persian original, signifying one to be revered; his excellency.

The style of the governor of Judea under the kings of Persia, always used with the article.

The Tirshatha ordered that those who could not prove their priestly descent should not eat of the most holy things.

Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah is expressly called the Tirshatha.

The word marks the province, not the kingdom; Judah had a governor where it once had a king.

Key Scripture

Ezr 2:63 — "And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim."

Neh 8:9 — "And Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha, and Ezra the priest the scribe, and the Levites that taught the people, said unto all the people, This day is holy unto the LORD your God; mourn not, nor weep."

Neh 10:1 — "Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah,"

Neh 7:65 — "And the Tirshatha said unto them, that they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and Thummim."

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this title. The principle to recover is that God's people have often lived under a legitimate civil authority that is not their own, and that faithfulness in such a season is neither revolt nor assimilation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Tirshatha is an archaic loan-word and nobody has contested it. What it sets against the present moment is the posture of the restoration community. Judah was governed by a Persian appointee under Persian law, paid Persian tribute, and rebuilt its wall by Persian permit — and Nehemiah neither pretended the empire was the kingdom of God nor treated his office as a compromise too dirty to hold. He took the commission, wept over the ruins, prayed to the God of heaven before he answered the king, and used a pagan power's authority to restore the worship of the true God.

The principle to recover is the ordinary Christian doctrine of the civil sphere. The magistrate is God's minister whether he knows it or not (Rom 13:4); Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the peace of the city; Daniel served three dynasties without eating their meat. What a believer under such an authority may not do is either of the two easy things — conclude that because the state is not Christian nothing may be done through it, or conclude that because something may be done through it the state has become the kingdom. Nehemiah signed himself the Tirshatha and kept praying for the throne of David.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tirshatha (H8660), governor, his excellency; pechah (H6346), governor of a province; medinah (H4082), province; 'Urim (H224) and Thummim (H8550), the priestly lots; golah (H1473), the captivity, the exiles.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tirshatha (H8660) — the Persian style of the governor of Judah.

Hebrew pechah (H6346) — governor; the ordinary Hebrew word Nehemiah also uses of himself.

Hebrew medinah (H4082) — province; what Judah had become under Persia.

Hebrew 'Urim (H224) — the priestly lot the Tirshatha waited for and did not have.

Hebrew golah (H1473) — exile, captivity; the community he governed.

Usage

"“And the Tirshatha said unto them” — a civil governor ruling on the holy things."

"“Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha” — the title attached to the man by name."

"“Till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim” — an honest confession of what was missing."
